office: Center for Drug Evaluation and Research (CDER)
subject: Warning Letter — CGMP violations, sterile drug products
content:
[SYNTHETIC EXAMPLE — fictional letter written for the WarnSync reference implementation. Not a real FDA record.]

Dear Ms. Alvarez:

The U.S. Food and Drug Administration inspected your drug manufacturing facility from January 13 to January 24, 2025. This warning letter summarizes significant violations of current good manufacturing practice (CGMP) regulations for finished pharmaceuticals. See 21 CFR parts 210 and 211. Because your methods, facilities, and controls for manufacturing, processing, packing, or holding do not conform to CGMP, your drug products are adulterated within the meaning of section 501(a)(2)(B) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act.

1. Your firm failed to thoroughly investigate any unexplained discrepancy or failure of a batch or any of its components to meet any of its specifications, whether or not the batch has already been distributed (21 CFR 211.192). Between June 2024 and December 2024, your quality unit closed eleven out-of-specification sterility investigations as laboratory error without identifying a laboratory root cause and without extending the investigation to other batches manufactured on the same line. Your investigation of the media fill failure of October 3, 2024 concluded that an operator intervention was responsible, but you did not evaluate the twenty-two commercial batches filled on that line before the failure was detected.

2. Your firm failed to establish an adequate system for monitoring environmental conditions in aseptic processing areas (21 CFR 211.42(c)(10)(iv)). Environmental monitoring data collected during the inspection showed recurring recovery of Bacillus species at sampling site FL-07, immediately adjacent to the filling needles. Your firm recorded thirty-one excursions at this site over nine months and, in each case, recorded the deviation without initiating a corrective action.

3. Your firm failed to establish laboratory controls that include scientifically sound and appropriate specifications, standards, sampling plans, and test procedures (21 CFR 211.160(b)). Your sterility test method was not qualified for the product matrix of your lyophilized product line, and your firm continued to release batches against that method after the method suitability failure of August 2024.

4. Your firm failed to ensure that the quality control unit had the responsibility and authority to approve or reject all components, drug product containers, closures, in-process materials, packaging material, labeling, and drug products (21 CFR 211.22(a)). Batch records for lots 24-0881 through 24-0904 were released by production supervision after the quality unit had placed the lots on hold pending investigation.

Corrective actions. In response to this letter, provide a comprehensive, independent assessment of your aseptic processing operations, a retrospective review of all sterility and media fill investigations closed since January 2023, and a remediation plan with timelines for your environmental monitoring program.

Failure to promptly correct these violations may result in legal action without further notice, including, without limitation, seizure and injunction.

5. Your firm failed to establish and follow appropriate written procedures designed to prevent microbiological contamination of drug products purporting to be sterile (21 CFR 211.113(b)). Your smoke study for the filling line was performed in 2019 under static conditions only. Video recorded during the inspection showed operators reaching over open containers to adjust the stopper bowl, an intervention not represented in your aseptic process simulation.

6. Your firm failed to clean and maintain equipment at appropriate intervals to prevent contamination that would alter the safety, identity, strength, quality, or purity of the drug product (21 CFR 211.67(a)). The sterilizing-grade filter housings on lines 2 and 3 showed visible residue at the time of the inspection, and your cleaning records for the preceding quarter were signed in advance of the operations they described.

Repeat observations. The deficiencies concerning investigation of discrepancies and quality unit authority were also cited at the conclusion of our January 2022 inspection of this facility. Your firm's response of March 2022 committed to a revised deviation management procedure and to quality unit sign-off on all lot dispositions. Neither commitment was implemented. Repeat observations raise questions about the ability of your executive management to allocate the resources needed for sustained compliance.
